item_name: Sensor Suite and Compute Platform Selection
competition_series: N/A - cross-team study spanning FSG, FS UK/FS-AI, FSAE Australasia, FSAE Michigan/Lincoln driverless classes
summary: Cross-team survey of FSAE/Formula Student driverless sensor and compute choices as of 2026. Teams converge on a small set of proven building blocks: a single 16-64 channel mechanical or MEMS LiDAR (Ouster OS0/OS1, RoboSense Helios, or the much cheaper Livox Mid-360; Velodyne Puck is no longer purchasable new since Velodyne's 2023 dissolution), 1-2 industrial global-shutter cameras or a stereo unit (Basler ace2, FLIR/Teledyne Blackfly S, or the all-in-one Stereolabs ZED 2i), a MEMS INS/GNSS unit for state estimation (SBG Ellipse, VectorNav VN-300, Advanced Navigation Certus, or premium OxTS RT3000 for well-funded veteran teams), and wheel-speed/steering Hall-effect sensors reused from the base EV electronics. Compute splits into two camps: NVIDIA Jetson (AGX Orin / Orin NX / Orin Nano) for low power draw and automotive-style thermal packaging, versus a custom x86 mini-ITX box with a discrete GPU for raw throughput and easier CUDA/PyTorch tooling (as used by Elefant Racing: Ryzen 3700X + RTX 2070 Super). DT.2.3 forces every sensor and DV electronics box to sit inside the chassis/tire outline or an approved aero zone, which is why almost all teams converge on a single centrally-mounted sensor pod near the roll hoop/nose rather than wide-baseline arrays. 2026 pricing is volatile: NVIDIA raised Jetson module/devkit prices up to 101% in July 2026, and Chinese LiDAR vendors (Hesai, RoboSense) face NDAA Section 164 and DoD 1260H-list scrutiny that does not block commercial/university purchase but adds import and reputational friction.
months_concept_to_first_autonomous_run: N/A - not a team metric. Cross-team pattern: sensor procurement to first validated sensor data on a bench is typically 4-10 weeks (dominated by LiDAR/INS lead time); bench-validated sensors to first data recorded on the actual vehicle is typically another 4-8 weeks once DT.2.3-compliant mounting and wiring are built.
months_concept_to_first_competition: N/A - not a team metric. Typical cross-team pattern: 3-5 months from finalized sensor/compute BOM to a fully calibrated, competition-ready sensor suite (procurement lead time + mounting fabrication + extrinsic/intrinsic calibration + on-vehicle validation runs), assuming no re-spins of the BOM.

what_slipped: Cross-team pattern, not one team's history: (1) LiDAR and INS/GNSS-RTK units are consistently the long pole - Chinese-sourced LiDAR (Hesai, RoboSense, Livox via grey-market resellers) adds customs/import delay on top of nominal lead time, and premium INS units (OxTS) can take 8-16+ weeks with factory calibration; (2) Jetson AGX Orin availability has been volatile - NVIDIA's July 2026 price hike (up to 101% on some SKUs) coincided with the official marketplace devkit going out of stock, pushing teams to third-party distributors at a premium; (3) teams that chose a discontinued or soon-to-be-discontinued sensor (Velodyne Puck, now unavailable new since Velodyne's Feb 2023 dissolution) got stuck sourcing used units or re-architecting late; (4) DT.2.3 envelope compliance is frequently discovered late - teams design a sensor pod for FOV/mounting height first and only then discover it protrudes outside the chassis/tire outline, forcing a mechanical re-spin.
platform_prerequisites: A running, race-legal EV chassis with a stable 24V-class LV bus and available DCDc capacity is a hard prerequisite before sensor/compute integration begins - the Elefant Racing case shows a dedicated DCU box drawing off a ~1000W DC-DC converter, sized generously above actual sensor+compute draw. Teams retrofitting DV onto an existing EV (rather than co-designing) typically need extra weeks to add a dedicated DV shutdown-circuit relay chain and DCDC capacity before any sensor bring-up can start.
ebs_design: N/A - covered in EBS-specific research; wheel-speed sensors used for EBS deceleration verification are part of this suite (Hall-effect wheel speed sensors, reused from base EV telemetry, ~$20-100/unit, days lead time).
steering_actuation: N/A - not this subsystem's scope; note only that a steering angle Hall-effect encoder (cheap, days lead time) is standard input alongside wheel speed for state estimation, as used by QUT Motorsport (QEV-3D) and Elefant Racing.
sensor_mounting_packaging: DT.2.3 requires all Driverless System components, sensors and cameras included, to sit either (a) inside the volume formed by the outside surfaces of the chassis and tires, or (b) within the permitted Aerodynamic Device locations (T.7.5-T.7.7). This rules out wing-mounted or wide-baseline sensor arrays that project beyond the tire envelope and is why the dominant pattern across teams is a single centrally-mounted sensor pod (roll hoop or nose-mounted), typically holding the LiDAR, 1-2 forward cameras, and GNSS antenna together. Elefant Racing mounted their two-camera + Nerian stereo system and antenna in enclosures replacing rear aero elements specifically because those slots are pre-approved DT.2.3(b) real estate; QUT Motorsport (QEV-3D) used a Velodyne Puck limited to a 180-degree field of view plus a ZED 2i, similarly pod-mounted. GNSS antennas need a rearward-facing or top-mounted position with sky visibility, which competes with the same DT.2.3 envelope.
mass_added: N/A - varies too much by build to state a single cross-team number; qualitatively, a Jetson-based build (compute + LiDAR + 2 cameras + INS + wiring/enclosure) adds roughly 3-6 kg [uncertain]; an x86 GPU mini-ITX build with equivalent sensors typically adds 6-10 kg [uncertain] due to PSU, cooling, and enclosure mass.
chassis_impact: N/A - covered in EBS/steering deep dives; sensor suite impact is mainly the need for a rigid, vibration-isolated pod mount point (often replacing an aero element) and routing for camera/LiDAR/GNSS cabling back to the DCU, plus a dedicated ventilated electronics box as used by Elefant Racing.
compute_platform: Two dominant patterns, both seen in the field: (1) NVIDIA Jetson family - AGX Orin (32GB/64GB module, up to ~275 TOPS, devkit officially $1,999-$3,499 depending on channel, now often listed higher after NVIDIA's July 2026 price increase of up to 101% on some SKUs; 15-60W envelope), Orin NX (8GB $399 / 16GB $599 module pricing post-hike, 117-157 TOPS, 10-40W), Orin Nano (8GB $249-$299, 40 TOPS, 5-15W) - chosen for low power draw, small automotive-style form factor, and built-in CUDA/TensorRT tooling via JetPack. (2) Custom x86 mini-ITX box with a discrete desktop GPU - Elefant Racing's Driverless Compute Unit used an AMD Ryzen 7 3700X + Nvidia RTX 2070 Super in a ventilated enclosure powered from a ~1000W DC-DC supply, chosen for full desktop-class CUDA/PyTorch compatibility and easier debugging at the cost of much higher power draw (150-350W GPU+CPU alone) and larger mass/volume. A dedicated safety MCU (e.g. an STM32-class microcontroller handling the shutdown circuit / EBS interlocks independent of the main compute) is common practice alongside either choice so a perception/planning crash cannot compromise the safety chain.
sensor_suite: Representative cross-team suite, synthesized: LiDAR - one unit, choice of Ouster OS1 (16/32/64/128-channel mechanical, ~$4,000-18,000+ per third-party reseller listings [uncertain exact 2026 official price]), RoboSense Helios-16P (~$3,285) or Helios-32/5515 (~$4,786), or the far cheaper Livox Mid-360 solid-state unit (~$480-550 via grey-market resellers, official-channel price likely higher [uncertain]); Velodyne Puck (VLP-16) is NO LONGER AVAILABLE NEW since Velodyne's 2023 dissolution/merger into Ouster and should not be planned around for a new 2026 build. Cameras - 1-2 industrial global-shutter units (Basler ace2/acA-series, Sony IMX-sensor based, used by Elefant Racing as 2x acA1920-40; FLIR/Teledyne Blackfly S, ~29x29x30mm, 3W draw, USB3 or GigE) or an all-in-one stereo unit, the Stereolabs ZED 2i (~$549-649 [uncertain 2026 price], built-in IMU/barometer/magnetometer, explicitly recommended by EUFS's 2021-2023 driverless lead as the go-to camera for new teams). IMU/GNSS/RTK - SBG Ellipse-N/Ellipse-D (dual-antenna INS, used by AMZ, Chalmers, TUfast, and QUT Motorsport per SBG's own FS case studies; price not publicly listed, ~$4,000-7,000 typical catalog range [uncertain]), VectorNav VN-300 (dev kit ~$5,000 confirmed; production unit likely $3,000-4,000 [uncertain]), Advanced Navigation Certus (Certus Spatial INS ~$3,190 confirmed indicative price), or premium OxTS RT3000 v4 (survey-grade, historically used by well-funded veteran teams like AMZ in early years; price likely $30,000-50,000+ [uncertain, not confirmed]). Wheel speed + steering angle - Hall-effect sensors, cheap (~$20-100 each) and short lead time, generally reused from the base EV's existing sensing.
power_budget: No single authoritative aggregate spec sheet found; synthesized from component datasheets and case studies [uncertain]. Vehicle LV bus is commonly 24V (confirmed by Elefant Racing's DCU description). Component draws: Jetson AGX Orin up to ~60W (MAXN mode), Orin NX 10-40W, Orin Nano 5-15W; a legacy NVIDIA TX2-class module drew ~15W; an x86 mini-ITX box with a discrete GPU (e.g. RTX 2070 Super class) draws roughly 150-350W under load; Ouster OS1-class LiDAR ~14-20W; Livox Mid-360 ~6.5W typical/8W peak; industrial cameras (Basler/FLIR) ~2-3W each, USB3/GigE bus-powered; SBG Ellipse / VectorNav VN-300-class INS ~1.5-5W. A Jetson-centric build's total DV electronics draw is roughly 150-250W all-in; an x86-GPU-centric build is roughly 350-600W all-in - this gap is the main reason Elefant Racing specified a 1000W DCDC converter with generous headroom for their GPU-based DCU.
shutdown_circuit_implementation: N/A - not this subsystem's primary scope; note that a safety MCU independent of the perception/planning compute is standard practice to host DV relay logic so a compute crash or reboot cannot silently disable the shutdown chain.

validation_strategy: Cross-team pattern for sensor validation: (1) bench power-on and driver/ROS2-node check per sensor; (2) intrinsic calibration (camera lens distortion) and extrinsic calibration (camera-to-camera, camera-to-LiDAR, all sensors to vehicle origin) - Elefant Racing streamlined this by measuring all sensor/antenna positions with a total station and digital inclinometers rather than hand-fitting a calibration routine; (3) static on-vehicle checks (cone placed at known distances, GNSS-RTK fix quality in the open); (4) low-speed dynamic runs comparing perception/INS output against a second reference GNSS-RTK rover recording ground truth, as done by both Elefant Racing (second RTK rover) and QUT Motorsport (simulator ground truth via EUFSsim before committing to on-vehicle testing, since vehicle time is the scarcest resource).
rules_compliance_challenges: DT.2.3's requirement that all sensors/cameras sit inside the chassis/tire outline or an approved aerodynamic-device zone is the dominant mounting constraint - it forces a single central sensor pod design pattern and rules out wide-baseline stereo or offset LiDAR placement that would otherwise improve depth accuracy or coverage. DD.1.2.4 (no map data given, no artificial landmarks) means the sensor suite must support fully real-time, memory-optional perception - a sensor/compute choice that assumes pre-built maps or fixed landmarks is a rules violation, not just a design inefficiency.
tech_inspection_experience: N/A - not sourced at the cross-team level for this deep dive; general pattern reported anecdotally in team materials is that sensor pods protruding past the tire/chassis outline (DT.2.3) and antenna/GNSS mast placement are common first-inspection flag points.
autonomous_speeds_achieved: N/A - context only: Skidpad/Acceleration speeds are typically 15-50 km/h for new teams (per Elefant Racing's stated 40-50 km/h acceleration / 15-20 km/h skidpad targets), which sets the minimum LiDAR/camera refresh-rate and INS update-rate requirements; QUT Motorsport's Nav2-based stack targeted up to ~30 km/h for Autocross/Trackdrive-style localization.
perception_range_achieved: By sensor, from case studies: monocular/stereo camera cone color+position detection typically reliable to 15-20m (Elefant Racing: 0.3-3m depth error for cones 10-20m out on a single camera; a 25cm-baseline stereo unit improved this to 0.4m error at 20m); Ouster OS1-class mechanical LiDAR nominal range ~120m at high reflectivity, though FSAE cone-scale reflective targets are reliably detected at shorter ranges in practice [uncertain, not independently confirmed]; Livox Mid-360 rated to ~40m detection range per official specs; ZED 2i stereo depth is rated usable out to ~20m outdoors.
reliability_notes: Common cross-team sensor reliability issues, synthesized: GNSS/RTK fix quality degrades sharply near buildings/trees (urban car-park testing environments, as explicitly noted as a confound in the QUT Motorsport ROS2 navigation paper, versus open competition tracks); LiDAR point clouds pick up rain/condensation noise; stereo camera depth estimation degrades in low light and at longer range (0.3-3m error band at 10-20m per Elefant Racing); vibration on a moving racecar is a real risk to any consumer/robotics-grade sensor not explicitly vibration-rated - teams generally add their own vibration-isolating mounts rather than relying on vendor packaging.
top_mistakes: Synthesized cross-team, not one team's claim: (1) choosing a compute platform on paper TOPS/spec alone without checking JetPack/ROS2 distro compatibility or software toolchain maturity for the chosen framework (PyTorch/TensorRT ARM builds on Jetson lag x86 releases); (2) under-budgeting LiDAR/INS lead time and discovering the shortfall only when mounting/calibration work is already scheduled; (3) designing a sensor pod for optimal FOV before checking DT.2.3 envelope compliance, forcing a late mechanical re-spin; (4) over-speccing an expensive INS/GNSS-RTK system (OxTS-class) when a MEMS-grade unit (SBG/VectorNav/Advanced Navigation) would suffice for Acceleration/Skidpad-level speeds - money better spent on redundancy or spares.
advice_for_new_teams: "You don't need a fancy IMU, or an expensive LiDAR" - Angus Stewart, 2021-2023 EUFS Driverless Software lead, writing in his 'How to Formula Student AI' post; he specifically recommends a stereo camera (ZED 2i, or whatever camera is already on the loaned ADS-DV platform) for cone detection and distance estimation, accepting that estimates will be poor at range but noting "at slow speeds it won't matter." General cross-team advice: buy sensors early given multi-week lead times, budget for a second/backup unit of anything with a single point of procurement failure, and prioritize a compute platform your software team can actually debug quickly (x86/CUDA familiarity often outweighs Jetson's power-efficiency advantage for a small, inexperienced team).
team_structure_dv: N/A - not a team. Cross-team note: sensor/compute integration (mounting, wiring, calibration, ROS2 driver bring-up) is typically owned by 1-3 people straddling the electrical and software subteams, distinct from the perception/SLAM/planning software effort covered in the companion research item.
recruiting_and_knowledge_transfer: Calibration procedures and mounting/extrinsics documentation are high-value, easily-lost institutional knowledge - Elefant Racing's approach of using a total station and digital inclinometers to directly measure sensor/antenna positions (rather than a bespoke calibration routine) is explicitly framed by the authors as reducing the software burden on a small, inexperienced team (C2/C3 in their design constraints: 40-60% of large teams' headcount, only 3-4 active software developers).
budget_estimate: Three rough tiers, synthesized from component prices above, all [uncertain] as aggregate figures since no team published a single itemized sensor+compute BOM total: Low-cost build (Livox Mid-360 ~$500 + 2x Basler/FLIR camera ~$800 + Advanced Navigation Certus or SBG Ellipse-D ~$3,200 + wheel/steering sensors ~$100 + Jetson Orin NX 16GB devkit ~$800) ≈ $5,400-6,000. Mid-tier build (Ouster OS1-32 ~$6,000-9,000 + ZED 2i ~$600 + SBG Ellipse-N with RTK ~$5,000 + Jetson AGX Orin devkit ~$2,000-3,500) ≈ $14,000-19,000. Premium/veteran-team build (RoboSense/Hesai industrial LiDAR ~$4,000-8,000 + dual Basler/FLIR ~$1,500 + OxTS RT3000 v4 ~$30,000-50,000 + custom x86 GPU compute box ~$2,500) ≈ $38,000-62,000, dominated by the INS choice.
recommended_sequence: 1. Lock compute platform decision first (Jetson vs x86) since it constrains ROS2 distro, driver availability, and power/thermal budget for everything downstream.
2. Order INS/GNSS and LiDAR immediately given their multi-week lead times, even before final mounting design is finished.
3. In parallel, design the DT.2.3-compliant central sensor pod and DCU enclosure, referencing chassis/tire outline and approved aero-device zones from the start, not as an afterthought.
4. Bring up each sensor individually on the bench (power, driver, ROS2 topic sanity check) before any integration.
5. Do intrinsic + extrinsic calibration with dedicated tooling (checkerboard rig, or a total station if available) once mounting is fixed.

6. Validate on-vehicle statically, then in low-speed dynamic runs against a second reference GNSS-RTK rover or known ground-truth track layout before trusting the suite for closed-loop autonomous control.
applicability_to_24_month_ramp: For a team starting June 2026 with a running EV and ~9 software-focused members, sensor/compute selection should be finalized and ordered within the first 4-6 weeks of the program given multi-week-to-multi-month lead times on LiDAR/INS and continued Jetson price/availability volatility - this is the single most schedule-sensitive procurement decision in the entire ramp. A lean, Jetson-based or single-camera-plus-cheap-LiDAR build (per siliconlad's explicit advice: skip the expensive LiDAR and fancy IMU) is more appropriate than a veteran-team OxTS/high-channel-LiDAR build, both for cost and because DT.2.3's compact-pod requirement rewards a simple, well-calibrated small suite over a complex, wide-baseline one. Budget contingency time and a backup vendor for the LiDAR/INS specifically, since a single-source delay there is the most likely critical-path slip in months 1-3.
